summary: Are you still with us: {the colleague} comes to be sure the player's vote is still theirs before the roll is called, and the player has to say yes, no, or not sure.
realLife: One life: In 2020 the Vermont House fell one vote short of overriding a governor's veto of a paid leave bill. Leaders said the member had signaled support the week before and was unsure on the morning of the vote while meeting the governor's staff; she said she had only been asking questions and never committed. Leaders called it a breach of trust. Another: Twelve senators held together for months to block a governor's appointee that needed a large majority, checking attendance all session and refusing to be called in one by one. The governor's office pressed them individually, and at the end of the session he vetoed several bills of the same senators; some suspected retaliation, others did not. Another: A senator of 89 asked the morning after a vote to reverse his position on a paid sick leave bill and an amendment, saying he had misunderstood. With the governor out of state and the margin thin, the other side delayed the revote until every member was in the room; observers did not know who had reached him.
gates: The vote record shows the player gave {the colleague} a word to vote a certain way, or the colleague counted the player's vote in on the record.
A vote on that matter is still ahead on {the body}'s calendar, or a repeat vote after a veto or a failed first try is.
{the colleague} has a stake in the outcome on the bill record: sponsor, manager, or a member whose own promise depends on it.
weights: How long and how close {the colleague} and the player have been.
How much the player's side needs the vote to hold.
Whether the player has since heard from the other side, from the governor's office or from voters.
Whether the player has told {chamber leader} of any doubt.
Whether the player's earlier word was said plainly or left loose.
choices: say yes plainly and mean it
say you are unsure and why, before the vote
ask what the colleague will do in return
say your vote is your own and leave it there

branches.when: the player confirms and the vote is cast as promised
branches.then: The promise on the record is kept, the favor owed to the player grows and {the colleague} says so at the next talk.

branches.when: the player says they are unsure and tells {the colleague} first
branches.then: The doubt is on the record before the vote; the tie takes a strain but not a break, and {the colleague} can still bargain.

branches.when: the player changes the vote without a word to anyone
branches.then: The broken promise is written when the roll is called; {chamber leader} and {the colleague} hear it from the floor, not from the player, and the tie falls hard.

branches.when: the other side or the governor's office is also working the player
branches.then: The talk turns on who the player answers to; the player's answer is read later by both sides.

branches.when: {the colleague} presses with a favor owed or a threat to a bill of the player's
branches.then: The pressure is written on the tie; the player's reply sets whether it is remembered as a plea or a threat.
